title: Transitioning from Electrical Engineering to Software
desc: A reflection on how my background in highly regulated fire safety systems translates to building reliable applications.

content.text: When I first began my career as an electrical engineer specializing in fire safety systems, I never imagined that the discipline and rigor required in that field would become the foundation of my journey into software development.
The Parallels Between Engineering and Code

Fire safety engineering and software engineering share a common DNA: both demand meticulous attention to detail, both operate under strict regulatory and quality constraints, and both require systems thinking—the ability to see how individual components interact within a larger whole.

In fire safety, a single overlooked wire or misconfigured panel can have catastrophic consequences. In software, a single unhandled edge case can bring down an entire system. This parallel mindset has been invaluable in my transition.
What I Brought to Software

My engineering background gave me a strong foundation in problem-solving, documentation practices, and systematic testing. These skills translate directly into writing clean, maintainable code and building robust architectures.
As I continue to share my journey at the intersection of electrical engineering and software development, I will be adding more detailed technical write-ups and reflections here.

title: Building Real-Time Social Networks
desc: Insights on using WebSockets and Go to create fast, scalable concurrent chat platforms.

content.text: Building a real-time social network from scratch is one of the most challenging and rewarding projects a developer can undertake. It touches every layer of the stack—from database design to WebSocket management to responsive UI rendering.
Why Go for Real-Time?

Go's concurrency model, built on goroutines and channels, makes it an excellent choice for handling thousands of simultaneous WebSocket connections. Each connection gets its own lightweight goroutine, keeping the code clean and the performance high.
Architecture Decisions
The GigaBit project taught me how to structure a social platform with real-time features including private messaging, group chats, typing indicators, and live feed updates—all powered by WebSockets.

title: The Architecture of Safety: Engineering Meets Code
desc: How the rigor of electrical testing and fire safety protocols informs system design in high-performance software.

content.text: The principles that govern safety-critical engineering systems have profound implications for how we design and build software. In this article, I explore the intersection of these two worlds.
Safety-Critical Thinking

Working with fire alarm systems taught me that every component must be tested, every connection verified, and every failure mode anticipated. This same mindset applies to building reliable software systems.

title: Complexity in Simplicity: The Art of Clean Code
desc: Why writing less code is often much harder than writing more, and how to master the art of minimalism.

content.text: There's a famous quote often attributed to Blaise Pascal: 'I would have written a shorter letter, but I did not have the time.' The same principle applies to code.
The Paradox of Simplicity
Simple code is the hardest to write. It requires deep understanding of the problem, thoughtful abstraction, and the discipline to remove everything that isn't essential.

title: Solar PV Systems: The Future of Energy Integration
desc: An overview of solar PV installation standards and the technical challenges of grid integration in Bahrain.

content.text: Solar photovoltaic systems represent one of the most promising pathways to sustainable energy. Having worked on solar PV installations in Bahrain, I've gained firsthand experience with the technical challenges and regulatory landscape.
Grid Integration Challenges

Integrating solar PV systems into Bahrain's existing electrical grid presents unique challenges, from voltage regulation to power factor correction. Understanding these challenges is essential for any engineer working in renewable energy.
Standards and Certification

The NOCN Level 3 certification and MEWA acknowledgment process ensure that solar PV installers meet rigorous safety and performance standards. These certifications are crucial for professional practice in Bahrain.
